seed_messages.speaker: Sarah
seed_messages.text: When people talk about consent, I think the interesting part is less the definition than whether someone can actually tell that a yes is freely given.

seed_messages.speaker: Mara
seed_messages.text: That makes me think about how awkward people can get when they want certainty from another person. Sometimes the pressure for a clear answer becomes pressure all by itself.

seed_messages.speaker: Owen
seed_messages.text: A useful distinction might be between obtaining an answer and establishing that the conditions around the answer were voluntary.

seed_messages.speaker: Jules
seed_messages.text: And those conditions are probably easier to notice in concrete situations than in abstract definitions.

message.speaker: sara
message.text: I wonder if the clearest sign is what happens after a no. If nothing gets colder, punitive, or strangely persuasive afterward, the earlier yes probably had more room to be real.

message.speaker: sara
message.text: There is another thing I keep noticing, though. We are talking about consent almost as if people inspect it from outside themselves. In an actual conversation, I suspect you often discover whether someone feels free by risking a little uncertainty yourself, rather than trying to eliminate it.
